Well, to be fair, it is pretty much part of any license agreement of companies that do tracking, so it's the users' own fault.

Should specify though that we are talking about typical tracking-data here, which is stuff generated and sent by applications - or in this case OS - during their usage, such as which buttons a user clicked in which order, which files he loaded, what happened before a crash etc., so encrypting the file-system would definitely not do anything against it. If you want to prevent it, you'd rather filter the respective traffic in your router.

I disagree about blaming the user for "clicking" the licensing agreement. Frankly, I do not agree with most everything that license states. Alas, the only way to use it is to "agree". Passing any law or enforceable action that is unavoidable is the hallmark of a perverse and corrupt system.

I'm glad someone else realizes this. It is far too easy for people to say, "lol use linux n00b," in reality that's impractical for a lot of people. I'm a Linux fan, but even I realize you can't throw WINE at your Windows applications, expect it to work, and call it a day, and there are innumerable other problems for that approach.
The solution might be either not to use it or to "tamper with" the product and to prevent the undesired mechanisms from functioning.

When every major software vendor requires telemetry in a non-negotiable (literal or practical) manner, and most regular users have software they need on these platforms and limited time, means, and flat-out talent to learn alternative systems, it is not their fault, and they are given the "choice" of having their data ransacked or not using a computer. This is a ridiculous trade-off, and a great way for government to erode our rights in general. We'll technically be free, sure. It's great to say that. But in practice, people are given a choice of live in a cave or get it up the ass with technology.

Frankly the behavior of these companies is reprehensible and cartel-like, but instead of price fixing, it's forced data theft.

And as an additional note, while you may be able to get Windows 10 Enterprise to deal with the telemetry, few can afford the ridiculous price for it and you shouldn't need to pay more just so you're not being spied on. The few Windows 10 controls that remain for consumer level editions are reset by mandatory updates (which is another problem), assuming the actual controls work in the first place.

Sure, it ain't right that they do this, but there is the choice to use free software, with a bit of convenience being the only price that is to be paid.

If you try to regulate these things by governmentally issued laws, you'll just end up loading a huge additional weight on the back of absolutely everyone who tries to distribute software legally and now would have to jump through numerous loops to get checked out and certified, and then it won't even do anything to multinational corporations who can just keep some make-belief headquarters in a nation that does not give a damn.

Control of data-theft is a bit like gun-control in that regard.
